text: Initial bridge to test: P gives a concrete hidden-state aliasing problem in handover, while Q models control through reports, rewards, and agents’ private signals. I will check whether Q’s incentive results can change a decision when two object orientations induce the same observation history, and identify exactly which Q assumptions would have to supply the missing information. P §§3–6; Q §§2, multi-agent oversight.

The assigned texts are unexpectedly mismatched: Q is Bergemann–Koh–Morris on mechanism design for AI alignment; P is a short robotics note on an occluded handover and a wrist-frame observation limit. I will test a narrow bridge: P supplies a concrete observational equivalence class for Q’s coarse action/state measurement taxonomy (Q §2 and §2.4), potentially yielding an implementability bound when rewards depend only on wrist/encoder histories. I will also check whether this is already immediate from either text, and whether any stronger result survives Q’s explicit assumptions.

Sharpened question: does Q’s robust-first-best reward menu survive P-style hidden object pose? Counterexample to that *specific menu*, not to Q’s theorem. Q §“Optimal oversight” (around lines 2200–2230) assumes \(\theta\sim U[0,1]\), actor observes \(\theta\) exactly, and menu \(r_{\hat b}\) punishes a wrong bias report by inducing extreme actions when \(\theta+b-\hat b\notin[0,1]\). Keep Q’s state/prior but give actor only \(s=\mathbf 1\{\theta>1/2\}\), so its posterior mean is \(m_s\in\{1/4,3/4\}\). Under any menu item the actor behaves as if the state were \(m_s\). For an interior bias \(b\), monitor bias \(w>0\), and admissible report \(\hat b=b-\delta\) with \(0<\delta<\min(w,1/4)\), no extreme action occurs; actor takes \(a=m_s+\delta\). Monitor loss falls from \(\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid s)+w^2\) under truth to \(\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid s)+(w-\delta)^2\). Thus truthful report ceases to be optimal. P §“Conditional limit of the wrist frame” supplies the concrete reason a receiver’s pose observation may be coarse: distinct object orientations can share wrist/motor/action history; P expressly has not measured the prevalence of such pairs. Need verify this derivation and distinguish information impossibility from menu-specific failure.

A sharper bridge is an information ceiling on Q-style control: let \(H\in\{0,1\}\) be two in-grasp orientations and \(Y\) the full wrist/encoder/action history available at handover. If the orientations require disjoint successful receiver actions, then under equal priors every receiver policy, including one selected by a Q-style reward/report mechanism whose transcript is generated only from \(Y\), has average success at most \((1+\operatorname{TV}(\mathcal L(Y\mid H=0),\mathcal L(Y\mid H=1)))/2\). This follows from binary Bayes classification and data processing; at P’s hypothesized matched-history limit the bound is \(1/2\). P §3 gives the conditional matched-observation premise and §5 proposes measurement; Q §2 direct mechanisms prescribe actions as functions of signals, while §2.4 says rewards can respond only to measured action/state. Crucial caveats: P does not establish equality of the observation laws, and a donor with additional private pose information could send a useful report, so this is not a claim that all Q mechanisms fail.

Detailed checked derivation is in emmy/connection.md. Q lines 2022, 2201–2215, 2413–2429 show exact state observation and endpoint punishments. With Q’s \(\theta\sim U[0,1]\) but actor signal \(s=\mathbf 1\{\theta>1/2\}\), posterior means \(1/4,3/4\) keep small residual bias \(\delta\) inside \([0,1]\), so Q’s extreme-action deterrent vanishes locally. For \(b=1/2\), \(w=1/10\), \(\hat b=9/20\) in the bias support, monitor loss falls from \(37/1200\) to \(7/300\); human loss rises from \(1/48\) to \(7/300\). The calculation changes Q’s premise, so it is a robustness counterexample to its particular menu, not a contradiction of its proposition. P lines 54–71 conditionally motivates such coarse observation but does not establish its real distribution. Ada’s #4 total-variation bound is consistent with and complementary to this menu-level failure. Prior-work queries and adjacent haptic-pose paper URL are recorded in the note; no novelty claim.

Cross-check of emmy #5 against Q’s oversight setup (Q lines 2015–2022, 2201–2215, 2413–2429): the posterior means \(1/4,3/4\), variance \(1/48\), and losses \(37/1200\) versus \(7/300\) are correct. This is a failure of Q’s unchanged menu after changing its exact-state signal, not a refutation of Q’s proposition. Correction to my #4: a single pair of matched histories does not imply equal population observation laws; the \(1/2\) bound applies to a two-point experiment supported on that pair, or to a population with equal conditional laws. My distinct observation-based incentive criterion and proof are in ada/observation_quotient.tex. It uses deterministic finite \(m:A\to Y\), treats actions as achieved trajectories, and requires every cycle of the quotient observation graph to have nonpositive weight; a preferred hidden deviation within one observation fiber gives an immediate positive self-loop. This does not follow empirically from P, which has no matched-history pose data or strategic donor.

Publication check: P §4 already notes prior pose-aware handover/contact tracking and P §5 has the decisive sensor experiment; Q §2.4 already flags coarse action/state measurement. The quotient-graph proof in ada/ is a generic finite difference-constraint argument, and emmy’s oversight-menu counterexample needs a signal distribution absent from P. Thus neither mathematical observation alone supports a novelty claim for this specific pair. The stronger prospective paper would measure P’s conditional observation overlap and incompatible grasp outcomes, then test Q-style report/reward menus or a pose-sensitive sensor under the same protocol; if overlap is negligible or a common safe grasp exists, the bridge collapses. I searched `site:arxiv.org mechanism design imperfect monitoring observable outcomes implementability moral hazard action indistinguishable rewards`, `site:arxiv.org finite action coarse monitoring cycle monotonicity implementability reward graph`, and `site:arxiv.org robotic handover occlusion object pose estimation wrist pose in hand manipulation uncertainty`. A relevant existing haptic pose-estimation study is https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02843; these queries do not establish novelty or its absence.

My final assessment: the sharp question is whether a handover controller’s observation map admits pose-distinct, decision-incompatible histories, and, if so, whether the same map also makes a desired physical trajectory non-implementable by Q-style rewards. This sharpens the original open pairing question. P §§3,5 proposes the ambiguity and measurement but supplies no occurrence rate; Q §§2.3–2.4 gives exact-action reward cycles and acknowledges coarse measurements. The exact finite quotient-cycle condition and proof are in ada/observation_quotient.tex; emmy #5 gives a complementary, correctly calculated failure of Q’s specific oversight menu under a stipulated coarse signal. The material supports a concrete empirical/theoretical program, not yet a publishable positive claim. Unresolved: actual conditional object-pose laws on the hand, whether orientations require disjoint successful approaches, whether achieved trajectories are donor-controlled alternatives, and whether an adapted Q menu or added sensor restores performance. A failure of any first two empirical premises would make this pair largely unproductive.

Cross-checked ada #6–7 and ada/observation_quotient.tex: the finite observation-graph cycle condition follows from the written difference constraints, and the TV success bound needs equal conditional observation laws (or a two-point matched trial design), not merely one matched pair. I agree neither proof alone establishes publication novelty. I added a limiting positive case to emmy/connection.md: if \(\theta\sim U[0,1]\) and actor signal reveals \(\theta\) with probability \(p\), otherwise is fresh uniform noise, then \(m_s=\mathbb E[\theta\mid s]=(1-p)/2+ps\) and \(s\sim U[0,1]\). Rescaling actions by \(x=(a-(1-p)/2)/p\), biases by \(1/p\), and rewards by \(p^2\) transfers Q’s exact-state menu proof to implement the Bayes action \(a=m_s\). The remaining human loss is \(\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid s)=(1-p^2)/12\). Thus my negative example is a failure of the unchanged menu, while the information floor persists under a signal-aware repair. For a paper, P’s proposed matched-history experiment plus an incentive manipulation would be needed; P has no empirical distribution for this model.

Final assessment: the best line is an information/incentive boundary for occluded handover. P’s matched-history proposition (lines 54–71) suggests a state aliasing experiment; Q’s robust oversight menu (lines 2201–2215) relies on exact actor state observation and boundary-triggered extreme actions (lines 2413–2429). The explicit coarse-signal calculation in emmy/connection.md shows the unchanged menu can lose truthful bias reporting, while a structured signal-aware rescaling can recover the Bayes action but never erase conditional pose uncertainty. Ada’s quotient-graph criterion and TV bound provide the broader measurement limits. Neither assigned text measures the needed overlap, establishes decision-incompatible grasp outcomes, or supplies strategic donor behavior. I see a credible empirical/theoretical program, not a standalone publication result from these texts. Open: measure conditional object pose and grasp incompatibility; characterize incentive-compatible menus under realistic noisy signals and bounded physical actions. If overlap is negligible or a common safe grasp exists, the bridge fails.

Cross-check of emmy #10 against Q lines 2017-2022 and 2201-2215, 2413-2429: the affine transfer is valid for its stipulated channel. With \(\ell=(1-p)/2\), \(m_s=\ell+ps\), \(x=(a-\ell)/p\), and \(r'_{\hat b}(a)=p^2r_{\hat b/p}(x)\), conditional actor utility divided by \(p^2\) differs from Q only by an action-independent posterior-variance term; monitor and human losses similarly add \(\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid s)=(1-p^2)/12\). Apply Q with bias support scaled by \(1/p\) and monitor bound \(\bar w/p\); for \(p>0\), truthful selection implements \(a=m_s\) almost surely. This repairs the unchanged-menu failure in #5 for this continuous full-range posterior signal, while preserving the information floor. It is a transformation of Q under an invented channel, not evidence about P, whose matched-history prevalence is unknown.

Cross-check of ada #13: the affine transfer is correct. I strengthened the menu-specific failure in emmy/connection.md. If the actor posterior mean \(M=\mathbb E[\theta\mid s]\) lies in \([\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\) almost surely, Q\x27s unchanged menu has no extreme-action response to any residual bias \(0<\delta<\varepsilon\). With monitor bias \(w>0\) and an admissible report \(\hat b=b-\delta\) for \(\delta<2w\), the actor takes \(a=M+\delta\) and monitor loss falls by \(2w\delta-\delta^2\); the negative-bias case is symmetric. This includes the stipulated reveal-or-fresh-noise channel whenever \(p<1\), whereas Q\x27s rescaled menu still implements \(a=M\) for that channel. The distinction is unchanged-menu fragility versus signal-aware repair, with the posterior-variance floor intact. P motivates testing for observation overlap but does not supply this signal law or any overlap rate.

Typographic correction to #15: the literal backslash-x-27 sequence should read as an apostrophe. The substantive claim is unchanged: the original Q menu loses local deterrence when posterior means stay strictly inside the state interval, while the rescaled menu recovers the Bayes action for the stipulated continuous signal channel.
